_comment: Training TRACKS: an ordered set of Library cards that travel together. A card joins a track by carrying {"track": {"id": ..., "n": ...}} in mission_templates.json. The track itself is described here so the Library can render one grouped card per track instead of nine loose ones, and so /api/track/<id>/all.zip knows what to build. Order is the `n` on each card, not the order here.

aar_boom.label: Air-to-Air Refuelling Academy — Boom and Receptacle (USAF)
aar_boom.premise: Eleven short rides that teach flying-boom refuelling the way it is actually taught — formation first, plug last. You start in position every time; the commute is deleted until ride 7, where it comes back on purpose. Ten of the eleven are graded in-mission — every ride except the operational capstone.
blurb: The receiver holds still and a boom operator flies the boom into the
receptacle. Your entire job is to stop moving. That is a formation
problem wearing a refuelling costume, and this track trains it in that
order: hold a position, control closure, then plug — not the reverse.

aar_probe.label: Air-to-Air Refuelling Academy — Probe and Drogue (Navy / Marine)
aar_probe.premise: Eleven short rides for probe-and-drogue — a different problem from the boom, not a variation on it. Nobody is helping: you fly a probe into a basket that is doing whatever it likes. Ten of the eleven are graded in-mission — every ride except the operational capstone.
blurb: There is no operator, no director lights and no calls. The basket does
nothing to help you, and staring at it is the failure mode. So this
track spends longer on the thing that actually works — flying formation
on the tanker and letting the probe arrive in your peripheral vision.

wk_checkout.label: 70th TFS White Knights — Squadron Checkout (F-4E, 1980)
wk_checkout.premise: Eleven rides from the three documents a new arrival at the 70th was handed in January and February 1980 — Standards, Low Level Training, and Weapons Information Sheet No. 1. Everything that makes you a wingman, and not a bomb between them. Ends when you are signed off on a two-ship.
blurb: The 347th was drafted into NATO contingency plans and never flew
to Europe in the Phantom. This is the war it was assigned, flown
as the plan. Your squadron's low-level contract meets a host
nation with its own floor, and the card prints both numbers and
tells you which one governs.

wk_proud_phantom.label: 70th TFS White Knights — Proud Phantom, Egypt 1980
wk_proud_phantom.premise: From 10 July to 3 October 1980 the 70th TFS flew twelve F-4Es out of Cairo West, Egypt. Ten rides from the squadron's Conventional Tactics guide of 27 January 1980 — five delivery planning sheets and ALL FIVE two-ship attacks, both halves of the split included — flown from the base they actually deployed to. The B'NAI is taught twice: once with a cue at every decision, once with nothing.
blurb: The B'NAI attack was designed by the Israelis in the 1973 war to
survive an SA-6 environment. Your squadron wrote it down five
months before it deployed here. Fly it on this map and you are
flying it over the ground it was invented on, with an SA-6 in
the mission.

cq_case3_f14.label: VF-101 Grim Reapers — Case III Night Recovery (F-14)
cq_case3_f14.premise: Five rides from CV NATOPS section 6.4: the marshal stack and holding to a time, the push and the descent gates, dirty up and the approach, the ball and the bolter pattern, then a night check in weather with every aid switched off. The Tomcat half — ICLS on the AN/ARA-63, Link 4 coupled through the nosewheel steering button, on speed at 15 units.
blurb: A night recovery fails in one of four places, and each has a
different cause. So this is one ride per gate, each starting where
the last one ended — you can fly the piece you keep failing ten
times in the span of a single full approach.

cq_case3_hornet.label: VFA-106 Gladiators — Case III Night Recovery (F/A-18C)
cq_case3_hornet.premise: The same five gates in the Hornet: ILS on the UFC, ACLS Mode I coupled in pitch and roll with ATC holding AOA for the throttle, on speed at 8.1 units. Marshal, the approach controller and Paddles do their half; the mission grades the half they ignore.
blurb: Supercarrier will let you push half an hour before your approach
time, descend at six thousand feet a minute and arrive at six miles
a hundred knots fast without a word. These rides grade exactly the
things it does not, and say so the moment they happen.

timing_f4e.label: Timing — The Clock on the Card (F-4E, 1980)
timing_f4e.premise: Four short Phantom rides from Fassberg that teach waypoint timing the way planners learn it — fly the card on a stopwatch, hit a fixed TOT, fit in behind a package on locked ETAs, absorb an early arrival with a hold — then a silent check ride. Every ride is graded in-mission.
blurb: Timing is anchored, not accumulated. One time is fixed — the
takeoff, the push, or the time on target — and every other number
on the card is solved from it. These four rides fix a different
one each, and the mission clock moves to make it true.
